Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient was also directly physically injured; that direct-injury theme is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Threat items center on personal physical danger and hypervigilance in the environment ('back to wall', exaggerated startle), which fits direct personal assault/combat trauma more than trauma to a loved one, and is not well linked to the reported appraisal content.

issues.item: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, this item implies an ongoing need to guard against immediate external danger to oneself. That does not fit well with the rest of the profile, which centers on bereavement-related cognitions (survival guilt, numbness) rather than personal threat exposure. It is also weakly aligned with the formulation, where Threat is linked mainly with Negative Appraisals and not with trigger-driven hyperarousal or ongoing danger monitoring.

The threat items are dominated by nonspecific hyperarousal and reminder reactivity, which usually implies trigger-linked activation, but the formulation specifies Triggers → Threat as inactive. With no trigger content present, 'physical reactions when reminded' is poorly aligned with the stated formulation structure.

'Mistrust: People can't be trusted' is a broad interpersonal appraisal that is not well anchored to trauma to a loved one in the rest of this profile. The other appraisal items center on guilt and emotional deadness, but pervasive mistrust suggests a different trauma pattern and lacks support from the selected threat items.

vignette: Mr. Tran, a 60-year-old South Eastern Asian fisherman, has been struggling with the aftermath of an event that forever altered his perception of safety and trust. About six months ago, during a routine fishing trip, Mr. Tran witnessed the tragic loss of one of his crew members when their boat capsized in heavy waves. The memory of that day is vivid for him; he still sees the panic on his colleague's face as they were swept away by the turbulent sea. Since then, Mr. Tran has experienced strong physical reactions whenever something reminds him of that stressful experience. Even the sound of rough water or the sight of a stormy sky sends waves of fear through him. These triggers are potent because he vividly recalls the terrifying moment when their boat capsized and his colleague vanished beneath the surface. Mr. Tran's fears have only deepened over time, as he has come to believe that people cannot be trusted. The thought that such an event could happen again, and that those around him might not care or be able to help, exacerbates his anxiety. His mistrust is a direct consequence of these strong negative feelings; every wave, every storm cloud, triggers intense fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame. He has also experienced significant emotional numbness since the accident. He often feels as though he's walking through life in a haze, unable to connect deeply with his surroundings or even his family. This sense of being dead inside is particularly troubling for him because it makes it difficult to enjoy activities that once brought him joy, like spending time at sea. Mr. Tran's guilt over surviving the accident when others did not has intensified these feelings. He carries a heavy burden of survival guilt, believing he should have done more to save his colleague. This sense of responsibility and remorse has made him increasingly wary and mistrustful of those around him, fearing that they might also be vulnerable or unreliable. The weight of these negative appraisals amplifies Mr. Tran's threat perception, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where every trigger brings forth stronger physical reactions and deeper emotional turmoil. His trust in others has eroded significantly, leading to increased anxiety and fear about future events. For instance, he often skips fishing trips, fearing that another accident could occur. This pattern of mistrust and heightened threat perception has strained his relationship with his wife and community. He avoids social gatherings and even fishing outings, isolating himself from the very activities and people who once brought him comfort and support. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a particularly severe episode where he experienced intense physical reactions after a recent storm warning on the local news. The anxiety and guilt became so overwhelming that he realized he could no longer continue living in this state of constant fear and emotional numbness. Mr. Tran is most afraid of not being able to reconnect with his loved ones and facing more traumatic events without support. He hopes for relief from these intense feelings, a way to regain trust in others, and the ability to enjoy life again without the constant burden of guilt and fear.
